“a nombre de” = under the name of
DNI is read letter by letter: “de-ene-i”. And “excelente” is read “eks-the-len-te”.
Recepción, habitación: stressed on “CIÓN”, with “th” in Spain.
They agree like adjectives: el segundo piso, la segunda planta.
“Primero” and “tercero” lose the -o before a masculine noun: el PRIMER piso, el TERCER día. But: la primera, la tercera.
After 10, Spaniards usually use ordinary numbers: el piso doce, el siglo veintiuno.
2. The impersonal “SE”: se habla, se puede
When it doesn’t matter WHO does the action, Spanish uses SE + verb in the 3rd person, where English uses the passive (“is spoken”) or “you / one”.
If the thing is plural, the verb goes into the plural: se vende un piso / se venden pisos.
To be more polite, you put the question “inside” another: “Where’s the lift?” becomes “Could you tell me where the lift is?”.
¿Me puede decir dónde está el ascensor?
¿Sabe a qué hora es el desayuno?
Quería saber si hay habitaciones libres.
For yes/no questions you use SI (if, whether), without an accent: “No sé SI hay sitio” = “I don’t know if there’s room”. Question words keep their accent: dónde, qué, cuándo.
I’d like to make a complaint.
“Quería” (the imperfect of querer) is a very polite way of asking, like English “I wanted / I was wondering”: “Quería una habitación doble” sounds nicer than “Quiero…”.
The staff’s answer: Disculpe las molestias (sorry for the inconvenience). Ahora mismo lo arreglamos (we’ll fix it right away).

El hotel de los mil errores
For their anniversary, Tom and Lena booked a weekend at a charming hotel in a village in Asturias.
On the website the hotel looked perfect: rooms with mountain views, an excellent restaurant and a pool.
They arrived on Friday evening after six hours in the car. There was nobody at reception.
They waited ten minutes. In the end a man appeared in his pyjamas. “Do you have a booking?”, he asked, half asleep.
He searched the computer for a long time. “It says here you’re coming next Friday,” he said.
Lena showed him the confirmation email. The man scratched his head. “All right, I’ll give you the last free room.”
The room was on the third floor. There was no lift. Tom carried the two suitcases up some very narrow stairs.
When they opened the door, they saw that instead of a mountain view, the room looked onto the car park.
On top of that, the shower had no hot water and the window didn’t close properly.
Tom was furious. “Tomorrow I’m going to make a complaint,” he said. But Lena was laughing: “It’s the worst hotel in the world! It’s perfect for a story!”.
The next morning they went down for breakfast. The restaurant was closed for the holidays and the pool was empty.
But in the kitchen they found an elderly lady, the owner’s mother, who made them fried eggs, homemade bread and an amazing coffee.
She told them the history of the village and recommended a secret trail through the mountains.
They did the walk and found a gorgeous lake with no tourists. It was the most beautiful day of the whole year.
In the end Tom didn’t write a complaint. He wrote an online review: “The hotel is a disaster. The lady in the kitchen is an angel. We’ll be back.”
A year later they went back to the same hotel. This time the booking was fine.
And the lady in the kitchen was waiting for them.
